rubrics.title: Lord of the Flies Final Essay Rubric

ratings.long_description: A clear, arguable thesis answers the central question and guides the whole essay.
A clear thesis answers the question; the essay mostly follows it.
A position is present but vague or drifts as the essay goes on.
No clear position, or the essay only summarizes the plot.
Three or more well-chosen, accurate moments or quotations, each clearly explained.
At least three pieces of textual evidence, most explained well.
Some evidence, but thin, vague, or left unexplained.
Little or no evidence from the text; claims unsupported.

criteria.description: Counterargument (states AND answers a strong objection)
criteria.long_description: Counterargument (states AND answers a strong objection)

Only one objection, or objections named but not really answered.

Hard to follow; frequent errors obscure the meaning.

assignments.title: Lord of the Flies Final Essay
assignments.html:
Lord of the Flies Final Essay
8th Grade ELA · Lord of the Flies
100 pointsEssay, 3 to 5 pages
The question
 
When the structures of civilization fall away, what is left of us: the better part or the worse?
Answer it through the novel. The worse part may win, the better part may survive in some boys, or what is left may depend on the person. Any of these can earn full marks if defended well.
The essay must
 
☐State a clear thesis in the introduction: one sentence that answers the central question and can be defended.
☐Prove it with evidence from the text: at least three specific moments or short quotations, each explained in your own words. Quote only from your own copy of the novel.
☐State and answer at least two strong objections. For each, name the best case a thoughtful reader could make against you, then answer it honestly.
Upload
 
Upload your essay as one file (.docx or .pdf, 3 to 5 pages).
LastName_FirstName_LOTFEssay_ELA8TypedCite by chapter
How this is scored
 
CriterionExcellentProficientDevelopingBeginning
Thesis & PositionA clear, arguable thesis answers the central question and guides the whole essay.A clear thesis answers the question; the essay mostly follows it.A position is present but vague or drifts as the essay goes on.No clear position, or the essay only summarizes the plot.
Evidence from the TextThree or more well-chosen, accurate moments or quotations, each clearly explained.At least three pieces of textual evidence, most explained well.Some evidence, but thin, vague, or left unexplained.Little or no evidence from the text; claims unsupported.
Counterargument
(states AND answers a strong objection)		Two strong objections stated fairly and answered convincingly with evidence.Two objections stated and answered, though one may be weaker.Only one objection, or objections named but not really answered.No genuine objection considered; only the writer’s own side appears.
Clarity & Correctness of ProseClear, well-organized prose; clean grammar, capitalization, and spelling.Generally clear and organized; few errors that do not distract.Understandable but uneven; errors begin to distract the reader.Hard to follow; frequent errors obscure the meaning.
Done when
 
☐My thesis answers the central question in one clear sentence
☐I have at least three moments or short quotations, each explained and cited by chapter
☐I stated and answered two strong objections
☐My essay is typed, 3 to 5 pages, and named LastName_FirstName_LOTFEssay_ELA8
☐My essay file is uploaded here

assignments.title: Q3 Recitation
assignments.html:
Q3 Recitation
8th Grade ELA · Lord of the Flies
10 pointsOne passageRecorded or uploaded
Choose one passage
 
Choose the passage you know best.
1
The conch passage (Chapter 1)
From “Ralph grasped the idea and hit the shell with air from his diaphragm.” to “the air over the island was full of bird-clamor and echoes ringing.”
2
The sea after Simon’s death (Chapter 9)
From “Somewhere over the darkened curve of the world” to “moved out toward the open sea.”
3
The closing lines (Chapter 12)
From “The tears began to flow and sobs shook him.” to “the true, wise friend called Piggy.”
Use the two phrases to find your passage in your own copy of the book.
Record it
 
30 to 60 secondsFrom memoryRecorder or file
1
Find a quiet space and face your device.
2
Say the passage from memory at a steady pace.
3
Record it here with the Canvas recorder, or upload a short audio or video file.
What we listen for
 
Accurate
CompleteThe words match Golding’s, in order, from memory.
Almost thereA few words were swapped, dropped, or read off a page.
Audible
CompleteClear and loud enough that every word is easy to hear.
Almost thereVoice dropped or trailed off so some words were lost.
Paced
CompleteSteady, unhurried, with pauses at the punctuation so the meaning carries.
Almost thereRushed or halting, hard to follow the sense.
10 when it is complete, 6 when it is almost there, 0 when nothing is turned in.
Done when
 
☐I chose one passage and said it from memory
☐My words are accurate, audible and paced
☐My recording or file is submitted here

discussions.title: Week 1 Discussion
discussions.html:
Week 1 Discussion
8th Grade ELA · Lord of the Flies
10 points1 post1 reply
Is Jack right?
 
“We’ve got to have rules and obey them. After all, we’re not savages.”
Jack, holding the conch (Ch. 2)
Will the boys keep order because of who they are, or only as long as their rules hold?
Post
 
4 to 6 sentencesCited by chapter
1Take a position on the question.
2Support it with one specific moment from Chapters 1 and 2, cited by chapter.
3Explain what that moment shows about the boys.
Reply
 
3 to 5 sentencesA classmate who disagreed
1Restate your classmate’s strongest point in your own words.
2Ask one question about their evidence.
3Say whether their point changes your view, and how much.
Done when
 
☐My post takes a position and cites one moment by chapter
☐My reply restates a classmate’s point fairly and asks one question
☐My reply says whether my view changed

discussions.title: The Island Assembly
discussions.html:
The Island Assembly
8th Grade ELA · Lord of the Flies
10 points1 proposal2 replies1 vote
The agenda
 
Your teacher opens the assembly with this agenda.
1
Goal. Agree on one rule that could have kept the boys together.
2
Deadlines. Your proposal by the first date your teacher posts; two replies by the second; your vote by the third.
3
Speaking limits. 150 words for a proposal, 75 for a reply, one sentence for a vote.
4
Hold the conch. One proposal each.
Proposal
 
Up to 150 wordsOne ruleCited by chapter
Chapter 8 ends with the boys split: Jack’s tribe along the beach, Ralph’s few by the fire.
1
Propose one rule the boys could have made on the platform, before the split, that might have kept them together.
2
Say which moment from Chapters 1 to 8 shows the rule was needed. Quote a few words from your own copy and cite the chapter, like this: (Ch. 5).
Replies
 
Two repliesUp to 75 words each
1
Reply to a classmate whose rule you would vote for. Summarize their rule in your own words, then add one more moment that supports it.
2
Reply to a classmate whose rule you doubt. Name the strongest part of their idea, then say courteously where it would break down on the island, with a moment.
Vote
 
One sentenceNot your own rule
1
Reply to your teacher’s agenda post with your vote: My vote: [classmate’s name]’s rule, because …
2
Your teacher posts the tally as the closing note.
Done when
 
☐My proposal is one rule, within 150 words, with a quoted moment cited by chapter
☐My first reply summarizes a classmate’s rule fairly and adds one more moment
☐My second reply names the strongest part of a classmate’s idea and disagrees courteously, with a moment
☐My vote is one sentence with a reason, for a rule that is not my own
